Core Belief If I treat teaching and learning as something to study, they do not behave like a simple natural law, where doing A always produces B. They behave more like statistical thermodynamics. Nobody can say where a single molecule will go next, but once the temperature and pressure are set, a large collection of molecules behaves in ways that can be predicted with confidence. Teaching looks like that to me. I cannot force learning to happen in any one student, but I can set conditions that make it more likely. In last year's statement I described learning through the second law of thermodynamics, which is itself a statistical law: left alone, things drift toward disorder. Deliberate learning runs against that drift, and it happens only when students and I both put effort in. That belief held steady over the past year. This year I focused on three variables: who my students are, how I teach, and, newest of all, AI. My Students My education specialist program taught me that community college students come from very different backgrounds. Teaching them showed me how wide that range really is. I have taught a student who took chemistry with us at high-school age and is now in a combined bachelor's and master's program in engineering at a four-year university. I have taught adults who already had careers and enrolled because they wanted to keep growing. Most of a section sits somewhere between those two. State policy widens the range further: since AB 705 and AB 1705, one section of CHEM V101 enrolls students whose math background runs from full fluency to foundational gaps. So I plan a course for that whole range from the first day, using the methods in the next section. Teaching Methods My goal is to make learning reachable, not effortless. That usually means putting an intermediate step where the gap is too wide, such as a simpler example before a complex one, or a worked line of reasoning students can see before they try it themselves. I also show the same idea in more than one form. For CHEM V101 lab there are 67 short videos of the experiments, and for lecture a library of 35 browser simulations I built this fall. At the bench, students get a checklist. For Experiment 2 this September, students ticked fifteen boxes while they worked, and every item on the next week's lab quiz traced back to at least one of them. The lab quizzes ask about the work done at the bench, because the lecture quizzes and exams already cover lecture content. The checklist also answers a point Malia Rose-Seisa made after observing my lab in 2023: students need to know exactly what to write down, and where. I also keep records. Through the Math Readiness Initiative I have been recording the exact point where students stop in a calculation: at a fraction, a ratio, or a unit conversion. That turns "weak at math" into something specific enough to act on, including whether two students with the same score are stuck in the same place. AI Who my students are and how to teach them have both been studied for many years. AI has not. Everyone is a beginner, new models arrive every few weeks, and a rule written in August can be out of date by October. As a user I find this exciting, and the AI Integration page covers that side. As a teacher, I learned quickly how little rules and restrictions can do on their own, so I went back to the learning itself. Students already know a good deal about how learning works. Without any training in education, they know that learning takes hours of practice. What they need is to connect that knowledge to the way they use AI. On the first day of lab I give them a one-page handout with three conditions for learning: cognitive friction, active recall over the illusion of competence, and productive failure. On the back, each student lists three ways AI helps learning and three ways it hurts, then swaps with a partner and tests the partner's points against the three conditions. In the first section that did this, the pooled answers arrived at all three conditions on their own, and the class AI policy was written from what students wrote. A standard built this way stays usable when the tools change, because what helps people learn has changed very little. Tracking Change Over Time To see whether any of this is working, I document much of what I do, from the notes behind a redesigned quiz to the records of where students get stuck. I also keep trying new things, especially ones that use what I am good at. Doing that for a year has changed how I read my own opening model. A statistical picture describes a system under one set of conditions at one moment. My teaching might be better described as a longitudinal study, where the same variables are watched as they shift from one semester to the next. Read that way, each semester is worth recording carefully, because the patterns I care about only show up across several of them.

CHEM V101 · Laboratory September 21, 2026 — Malia Rose-Seisa Strengths noted. The lab began on time, with students signing in at the instructor's desk. The opening slides listed the equipment and learning objectives and included photographs showing how to read a meniscus and where to measure from on a ruler. During the briefing, students located the revised step in their lab manuals, then moved straight into paired work while I circulated to check sign-in and safety gear and answer questions. A lab checklist laid out each step, what to record and calculate, and what students should be able to explain afterward. Areas for improvement. Have students copy the equipment list and objectives into their notes. Carry demonstration items around the room so every student can see them, and walk the lab far more, both between the aisles and around the perimeter, so every student stays on the same page; one raised hand in the back row went unnoticed. Make sure students actually estimate the last digit when reading a volume. Clarify how the checklist is meant to be used, whether it is turned in or kept, and whether some steps might be better left for students to work out on their own. CHEM V101 Late Start · Lecture October 5, 2026 — Jeffrey Wood and Russ Frohardt Strengths noted. The observers highlighted clear expectations about what to memorize for the next test, well-placed questions throughout, and clear worked examples for naming ionic and molecular compounds. The slides were easy to read, and the use of zooming was described by one observer as "masterful and dynamic" and by the other as an "amazing use of technology." Starting in Fall 2025, lecture and lab were combined under a single CRN. A course whose lecture and lab had different instructors now had to run out of one Canvas shell and one syllabus. I saw that as a chance to work with the other instructors on a smooth transition. The steps are below. That fall I taught the lecture for two linked courses. In CHEM V101 (CRN 70961) the lab was taught by Zhibang (Jim) Duan. In CHEM V104 the two lab sections were taught by Antonia Flores (71293) and Crystal Serrano (71290). The linked format has continued since. Step 1 — The department meeting (April 2025) On April 18, 2025, the chemistry department held a department meeting on how lecture and lab would be integrated for Fall 2025 and how the shared Canvas shells would work. Two of its decisions apply to the linked courses: Lecture instructors would set up and maintain the shared Canvas shell. Lab instructors would be added as co-instructors, mainly for grading and due dates. The final grade would be split between lecture and lab by unit count rather than a fixed percentage. For CHEM V101, a four-unit lecture with a one-unit lab, that meant 80:20. Several questions were left open, including minimum passing grades for each component, make-up labs, and how to grade late work. The reasoning in the room was that other departments already weighted their labs this way. Physics and microbiology, with one-unit labs, give the lab 20–25% of the grade. We agreed to try the unit rule for a year and adjust it if it did not work. Because I was teaching the lecture for both V101 and V104 that fall, I wanted the details settled early. Lab quizzes in CHEM V101 are ten multiple-choice items on paper, taken in class about a week after the experiment they cover and graded on ZipGrade. Each experiment has one. I wanted these quizzes to focus on the hands-on experience (the work at the bench and what the student had to account for in writing the report) rather than repeat lecture content. The lecture quizzes and exams already cover that material. The reason was practical. At the time, the lab and lecture sections of a course were often taught by different instructors. A quiz drawn from lecture material asked a lab instructor to grade content they had not taught, on a schedule they did not set, and it returned nothing about what had happened in the lab. Typical questions: How much deionized water went into each well of the spot plate? (Exp 1) Which reagent was added first, to test for barium? (Exp 5) Why must the baseline and the sample dots be marked in pencil rather than pen? (Exp 11) What did you record as the initial buret reading for Trial 1? (Exp 16) A student who was at the bench and wrote their own report can answer these. A student who skimmed the manual cannot. I hold to two things in writing them. A quiz should register whether a student took part in the experiment, and catch the one whose partner did the work. And it should not ask what a student's own sample looked like. An experiment that failed should not cost points; the question asks what the test shows when it works. I revise the quizzes as the course changes. Before and during Fall 2026 I rewrote two of them, one because it had a question written against a lab manual no longer in use. For Experiment 2 this fall I also gave students a one-page checklist to mark during the experiment. It has fifteen boxes arranged by the parts of the procedure, and each of the ten questions on that experiment's quiz corresponds to at least one box, so a student who works through the checklist at the bench has already met what the quiz will ask.

Most of the tools on this page came to me from colleagues, from trainings, or from the teaching literature. I took each one far enough to see how it fit my courses: in some cases by building with it, in one case by watching it in a colleague's classroom. MyOpenMath Colleagues who already used MyOpenMath for CHEM V101 recommended it, and it is the tool I spent the most time on. I used it two ways. CHEM V120B: pre-labs written and run. For the six-week Summer 2026 term I moved the pre-labs for all ten experiments out of the lab notebook and into auto-graded MyOpenMath assignments. Students had three tries per question, saw their score on each question immediately, and saw the answer and a short explanation after the last try. Grades reached Canvas through LTI, the standard link that lets Canvas open an outside tool and record its grades. Questions in MyOpenMath are written as code, and at first I counted that in its favor. A question written as a script can be drafted by AI, so work I would otherwise do by hand could be handed over, and not knowing the platform's language was no obstacle. I used Claude to draft the code for each question from the lab manual and to check every numerical answer by calculation. The difficulty was getting the code into the platform. MyOpenMath has no API, meaning no way to send files to it directly, so the code for each question had to be copied and pasted in by hand, tested in the preview, and corrected. The format took five rounds of that before it held, and the other nine experiments were built from the first as a template. Browser tools that let an AI do the entry have since made the copying easier, though MyOpenMath is still comparatively unfriendly to work with. CHEM V101: a full course, set up but never connected. In May 2026 I set up a V101 course for Fall 2026 from a colleague's existing course, with homework for Chapters 1–14 in 23 assignments. Before committing, I checked the homework against my ten quizzes, since my worksheets cover more than the quizzes test. The gaps were small, and I accepted them. Decision. Students did not raise problems with it. The costs were on my side, in entering the questions, in editing a question once it was live, and in late work, where a student who needed more time had to spend a LatePass, the platform's built-in extension token. Sharing, one of the reasons I chose it, did not work the way I expected. A colleague warned me that an assessment copied from another instructor's course stays tied to that instructor's class, and a Canvas export of a MyOpenMath course carries only the links while the questions stay on the MyOpenMath server. Nothing I was asking students to do required MyOpenMath. After the summer term I did not continue with it, and I did not connect the V101 course. The quiz feature in Canvas may be the better home for the pre-labs. It does the same job inside Canvas, any colleague can copy it, and it can be built from a script through Canvas's API, so I may move the pre-labs there. Plickers Plickers lets an instructor check understanding without student devices. Each student holds up a printed card with a code on it, and the way the card is turned marks their answer. The instructor scans the room with a phone or tablet and sees every answer at once. Seeing it run in a colleague's classroom, I thought it was a good tool, both in what it can do and in how smoothly it worked with a real class. I looked at how I could use it in mine. It can be done. I already use my iPad to run and annotate my lecture slides, so scanning the room would mean a second device or handing the slides off for that moment, and I was unsure the extra step would be efficient enough in my lectures to try it right away. I have not used it in my own class so far. In-lecture demonstrations Joe Selzler suggested that I try demonstrations in lecture. When I asked him where to start, he lent me two volumes of Bassam Shakhashiri's Chemical Demonstrations and told me to look there. I also bought the American Chemical Society's Chemical Demonstrations: A Sourcebook for Teachers (Volume 2). The one I ended up running came from a video I found on YouTube while I kept looking: three flasks with the same amount of acid and increasing amounts of baking soda, and balloons that stop growing once the acid runs out. It ran in October 2025 and is described on the CHEM V101 Lecture Demonstration page. I did not add more. Preparing a demonstration took real time, and stopping for one broke the flow of the lecture. It also made me settle how I divide lab and lecture. In my courses chemical demonstrations belong to lab, and in lecture I want the time to go to the lecture content. For lecture, the form of demonstration I settled on is the interactive simulations, which are on the CHEM V101 Interactive Simulations page. PlayLab In Spring 2026, through the college's AI Community of Practice, I used PlayLab to build a project guide for a CHEM V120B final project. The project is long and has many steps. Students audit the claim that a protein structure is "known." They collect a corpus of 400-plus sources, draw one to three checkable claims from each, and verify the claims against experimental metadata and prediction-confidence metrics. In the first week, before any collection begins, they write inclusion and exclusion rules and a bias prediction, a statement of what they expect their own sources to over-represent. The guide keeps track of where a student is in that sequence. It checks whether each step has been done, and when a student asks what to do next, it points to the next step. Its knowledge base is three documents I wrote: the course AI policy, the AI-use disclosure form, and the project handout. Following that policy, it helps with brainstorming, drafting and formatting, and it leaves interpretation and final conclusions to the student. The guide and the project have not been used with students, and the guide remains a prototype. Four things kept me from taking it further. PlayLab does not integrate with Canvas. Using it would require an activity or assignment that makes students work inside PlayLab, and I was not convinced a course requirement should be built around a tool. It keeps no log of student use that I can collect, which makes anything students submit from it awkward to handle. Finally, the scale did not work. What I want from AI in a course is a project at a scale only AI makes possible, but as the project grows the model behind the guide struggles to handle it, and cutting the project down to what it handles well leaves little worth doing.

Where the Calculation Breaks: Four Failure Patterns in Introductory Chemistry Problem Solving Referred to throughout this portfolio as the Math Readiness Initiative. Placement policy and the classroom it produced California's AB 705 (2017) substantially restricted placement assessment and enforced prerequisites at community colleges; AB 1705 (2022) further limited remedial coursework before transfer-level enrollment. As a result, a single section of CHEM V101 now enrolls students whose mathematical preparation runs from full arithmetic fluency to foundational arithmetic gaps, a population that prior policy would have partitioned across several course levels. In class, students now stop before the chemistry begins, at a fraction, a ratio, or a unit conversion the course has always been able to assume. Across those years math readiness came up in chemistry department meetings again and again, and the concern kept growing. The change is structural, and the teaching methods of the previous decade were not designed for it. Analysis at a finer resolution "My students are weak at math" was too abstract for me to act on, and so was a course pass rate. I wanted the problem at a resolution where I could see which students break, where in a problem they break, and whether two students with the same score are failing the same way. The material to look that closely was already mine. I record every lecture through Zoom and it transcribes automatically, so by 2026 I had more than a year of lecture text. Quizzes and assignments are scanned and submitted digitally through Canvas, which had accumulated into several years of student written work. Both had only been stored, because reading that volume by hand would take more time than a teaching load leaves. An analysis tool that applies the same rubric consistently across all of it is what made the closer look possible. Method The chapter-by-chapter demand map. Before looking at student work I went through my own lecture materials chapter by chapter and wrote down the specific operations each one requires a student to compute. That inventory, across CHEM V101 chapters 1 through 12, produced a set of six skills the course keeps asking for, which I then reviewed and fixed as the working list. Core skill Where CHEM V101 asks for it Dimensional analysis Ch 2 (metric), Ch 6 (g ↔ mol), Ch 8 (stoichiometry), Ch 11 (gas stoichiometry), Ch 12 (heat) Proportional reasoning Ch 2 (density), Ch 6 (percent, mol), Ch 8 (stoichiometric ratio) Scientific notation Ch 2 (introduction), Ch 6 (Avogadro's number), Ch 9 (wavelength calculation) Algebraic rearrangement Ch 7 (oxidation number), Ch 11 (PV = nRT), Ch 12 (Q = mcΔT) Understanding percent Ch 6 (percent composition), Ch 8 (percent yield), Ch 11 (partial pressure) Multi-step decomposition Ch 6 (empirical → molecular), Ch 8 (stoichiometry), Ch 12 (heating and phase change) In the right-hand column the same few skills reappear under different chemistry headings. A student who is shaky in one of them meets it again every few weeks in a different chapter. Coding the student work. This analysis was prepared as material for a chemistry department meeting on math preparation in May 2026, on records from my own course; the manuscript came out of it afterward. Spring 2024, CHEM V101, a single section: 54 students, with the full written-work archive across six assessment assemblies. Every response is sorted into five categories (correct; magnitude or unit error; partial execution; no work shown; setup only), and what identifies a student is the pattern across their responses rather than any single score. I wrote the five-category codebook; a language model applied it to each exam and proposed a first-pass type along with its reasoning; I reviewed every classification and held final say. The model applies my codebook at a scale one instructor cannot reach by hand. The name area on each scan was blacked out before any file was processed, so no student's name reached the model. Four students read in depth. The initial intent was to code all 54 for population-level statistics. Four students were read in depth instead, across multiple assessments. They were chosen from the gradebook before any written work was opened: one from each band of the score distribution, top to bottom, with attention to how each student's scores moved from one exam to the next. Sampling across the whole distribution kept the low end of the class from defining the framework. The working frame at that point was a two-way split between a skill gap and a processing gap. The four types came out of the readings afterward, and the division inside Type 2 appeared only while those readings were under way. Of the other 50 students, the 48 whose Exam 2 free response was on file were then coded on that single assessment to see whether the same types recurred. Types 1 and 2a did. Type 2b produced no instances in that pass, which is a limit on how far the framework has been confirmed and one of the things a larger collection is meant to settle. Reading the lectures against the types. Once the types existed, I checked whether my own lectures reach each of them. Twenty-one lecture sessions from Spring 2026 were transcribed and read along seven observation dimensions drawn from the same framework, among them whether steps are named and carried values verified, whether problem categories are identified before procedures run, and how much of the session is student work time. The rubric is built to surface shortfalls, so a dimension that comes back as reached is a minimum. The lectures were also designed before the types existed, which keeps the exercise from grading a lesson against the framework it was built from. Findings The course asks for three different things. Layer What it is A · Prerequisite arithmetic Fractions, ratios, proportional reasoning, unit conversion — the layer AB 705/1705 most directly affects. B · Math in chemistry context Stoichiometric ratios, dimensional analysis as structure, formula rearrangement. C · Multi-step execution Tracking intermediate values across a problem chain. Students break at four different places. Each type is defined by where in the chain the breakdown occurs, rather than by the score it produces. Four failure types mapped against prerequisite math fluency and execution or self-monitoring: Type 1 is a prerequisite cascade, Type 2a stalls mid-step, Type 2b drops the last step, and the baseline learner's self-checks hold. Illusory comprehension is a risk across all four types, highest for Type 1 (see the table below). Type Failure locus Risk of illusory comprehension Instructional lever Type 1 · Arithmetic Gap Layer A is not automatic. Arithmetic consumes working memory before the chemistry arrives — a cognitive-load cascade upstream of the chemistry itself. High Automaticity training (Cover-Copy-Compare); reduce working-memory load before the chemistry starts. Type 2a · Monitoring Gap Layers A and B hold. Execution collapses between steps in Layer C: intermediate values are lost as the chain lengthens. Moderate Visual roadmap and scaffolding with explicit carry-over verification. Type 2b · Transfer Gap Layer B is intact within a familiar problem category. Under a novel context the retrieval cue fails before the math begins. Low Interleaved practice, plus a final-step metacognitive prompt. Baseline · Fluent Learner The chain completes. A framework has to account for who is underserved at the top as well as who is failed at the bottom. Low Peer-led structure and verbalization: the fluent student as explainer, not recipient. Illusory comprehension (following a worked example and taking that for the ability to execute one) is the third column of the table. It runs across all four types and raises the cost of each, and it is highest where the arithmetic itself is still expensive. The table is a second version. The one I presented to the department in May 2026 sorted each type by which layer was the problem. Reading more cases made a finer question answerable: which layers hold, and where the chain breaks. Type 2b moved the most. It first looked like a collapse in multi-step execution, and the later readings showed a retrieval failure with the chemistry-context math intact, which is what separates it from Types 1 and 2a. Colleagues who saw the May slides will find the assignments above differ from them for that reason. Every lever in that last column comes from existing research. What the analysis adds is which one to reach for, because the four types respond to different ones. One quiz, two students, opposite patterns. The clearest case in the Spring 2024 archive is a single Chapter 6 quiz (percent composition, moles, empirical and molecular formula). Two students scored 11 out of 20 and 15 out of 20: close enough that a gradebook groups them together and gives them the same advice. Quiz 5, page 2, from the student scoring 11 out of 20. Question 5 asks for empirical and molecular formula; the answer box holds a formula with no work shown, and question 4 holds a number with no work shown. The first student answers in bare numbers. On the reverse-percent item the setup is right and the result is off by a factor of one hundred; on the Avogadro items the units stay in grams where the question asked for molecules; on the last item a formula appears with none of the steps that would produce it. The tools this student needs (dimensional analysis, scientific notation, percent run backwards) are prerequisites the chemistry depends on (Type 1). The same page from the student scoring 15 out of 20. Question 5 shows the full worked procedure — each element's mass percent divided by its molar mass, normalised to the smallest value, multiplied up to whole numbers — arriving at the empirical formula, with the molecular formula step absent. The second student's work is visible from beginning to almost-end. The molar-mass divisions, the normalisation, the multiplication to whole numbers are all on the page, and the empirical formula is correct. The molecular formula step is missing. The same thing happens on the Avogadro item: the conversion is set up correctly, the arrow to the final unit is not drawn. The mathematics is in place; what is missing is a structure that forces the last step (Type 2b). The two students took the same quiz, earned close scores, and need different help, which is why I sort by failure locus instead of by score. A lesson can be well taught and still not reach a given student. Reading the transcripts showed that breaking a problem into labeled steps and checking the carried value at each one (what the literature calls step-labeling scaffolding) is something I do often and do at high fidelity. That is the right move for the student who holds the chemistry but loses intermediate values as a problem lengthens (Type 2a). The same transcripts show a gap at the other end: the fluent student who learns most by explaining to a peer gets few openings to do it. Both readings come from my own lectures, and what they measure is whether the mechanism a student needs was present, which is a separate question from how well the hour was taught. Journal submission By 2026 the material had accumulated into something already shaped like research (a documented framework, a codebook, a classifier, supporting materials), and I decided to develop it into a paper. A manuscript went to the Journal of Chemical Education on June 25, 2026 and was rejected on August 10. The rejection came on three grounds, and two of them are about the study. The first, the editor's primary one, was scope against evidence: a single manuscript proposed a classification framework, argued its validity, drew instructional implications and recommended interventions, while the framework itself came from a small number of cases. The second followed from it: intervention effects belong in a study of their own, and a resubmission should concentrate on the empirical validity of the framework: more data, the coding process documented, inter-rater agreement, the instructional implications lowered from conclusions to hypotheses. The third was institutional: ethical approval and participant consent had to be addressed. The work had been conducted as ordinary analysis of my own teaching, without the approval structure that publication requires. I paused the research the same evening. The preparation already under way. A second study, a fall collection with consent, had been in preparation since spring, and it needed a review board. In late May I wrote to the IRB at California State University Channel Islands, which replied that it could not review external researchers without a formal agreement between the two institutions. In July I took the study to an independent review board, Solutions IRB, completed the human-subjects training it recommended, and wrote what a submission requires: a study protocol, a consent form, parental permission and assent forms, recruitment materials, and a syllabus statement. The application was assembled and had not been submitted when the research paused. The college's review procedure. Ventura College has no Institutional Review Board, and when I brought the question to the Dean of Institutional Effectiveness, what came back was that faculty research with district students had essentially not happened outside doctoral programs. There was no established route to point me down, because nobody had needed one yet. We met on August 12, 2026 and settled four things: the research is paused; analyzing my own teaching and sharing it within my department remains ordinary instructional work; any future publication route requires a written proposal with consent and permission materials, approved before anything begins; and the Dean would assemble a process checklist for conducting research with district students, run it past the deans, and publish it. On August 31, 2026 that checklist was published. It is on the college website, and its first lines state the position plainly: Faculty, staff, and/or external groups who wish to conduct research on VC students or employees must receive campus approval prior to collecting data. Ventura College does not have an Institutional Review Board (IRB). Thus, as part of this process, approval must be obtained from an accredited external IRB. It then sets out seven requirements: federal human-subjects training and FERPA training, both within two years; an executive sponsor at dean level or above who agrees the work benefits Ventura College students or employees; approval from an accredited external IRB, with conditional campus approval available when the external board wants to see campus approval first; submission of the completed forms to the Dean of Institutional Effectiveness; that Dean's approval; and review by the college's Executive Team. I am its first user. The human-subjects training I had completed in July turned out to be a different course from the one the checklist names, so in September 2026 I completed the one it names, along with the FERPA training. The executive sponsor is the requirement still open. The collection this project needs is designed around the rejection's main objection — two terms, Fall 2027 and Spring 2028, rather than a single term, a sample several times larger, and inter-rater reliability built in from the start, with Crystal Serrano as independent co-rater. Students write a study code, not their name, on the pages that get scanned, so the files that are processed carry no names. The procedure was not on the college website when we met in August; it is there now, and the next faculty member can follow it. Fall 2026 implementation and current status The four types are what this fall's CHEM V101 is built around. Five interventions sit in specific chapters, each attached to the students it is meant to reach: an automaticity warm-up for the student whose arithmetic still costs attention; a three-step check on units, significant figures and plausibility; a mole-map scaffold; interleaved retrieval practice for the student who can do the math inside a familiar problem and stalls when the context changes; and a peer teach-back, placed in the chapters where explaining carries the concept, for the fluent student who learns by teaching. The record of what happened on a given day comes from the recording rather than from memory. A codebook sets what counts as an intervention having run, and it asks for a verbatim line from the transcript as the evidence. Each session's entry notes what was planned, what ran, how continuous the recording was, and what I promised students I would do. The record also showed that the peer teach-back happens when a practice block opens, which is different from where I had placed it on paper. On the days a problem set opened, it happened; on the days it was scheduled inside a lecture segment, there was no opening for it. The course runs twice each term, in a full-term section and a later-starting one, which makes the second run a place to change one thing deliberately. I write those change plans before the class. The first of them concerns a control variable: in the full-term run it was excluded from both lecture and practice quiz; in the later run it is taught and the quiz is announced in advance. One limit is built into the record. The lecture captions label every line as the instructor, so student talk the microphone picks up cannot be told apart from mine. What students said during a peer teach-back cannot be recovered from these recordings, and a day with no entry means the recording does not show it. As of now the manuscript is not under review anywhere and no resubmission is in progress. The pause lifted on August 31, when the college published the procedure; what remains is the approval itself, and the open gate is the executive sponsor. Data collection is planned for Fall 2027 and Spring 2028, once the approvals are in place.

Over the past few years, AI has become one of the most talked-about topics at the college. Like everyone else, I was starting from scratch. In the beginning, "using AI" just meant typing questions into a chatbot. As new models appeared and the information around them grew, I kept trying new things. This page is a record of what I've tried along the way. Understanding different levels of AI use Google DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts the three-dimensional structures of proteins, work that earned a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Meanwhile, my own use of AI during my first years here amounted to typing questions into a chat window. The gap between the two bothered me. But I wasn't going to become an AI engineer overnight, and I wanted to understand what the steps in between looked like. In April 2026, Michal Klacko of STRV published a framework that divides AI use into six levels: Skeptic, Tourist, Assisted Coder, Prompt-Driven Developer, AI-Native Engineer, and AI Architect. It was written with software developers in mind, and since I'm not one, the categories didn't mean much to me at first. As I got to know these tools better, though, I found I could draw my own lines based on what the work involves: Level 1 — Chatting. Asking questions in a chat window on an AI website. Level 2 — Organizing work into projects. Instead of separate chats that each start from scratch, the conversations and files for a larger task live together, so every new chat already has the task's context. Level 3 — Working on my own computer. AI runs as a desktop application with access to local files and programs, so it reads and edits the actual documents rather than me copying text in and out of a browser. Level 4 — Building a personal knowledge system. Material is stored and organized systematically, in a form that both I and AI agents can find and use. Level 5 — Connecting and automating. AI connects directly to websites and services, and I build tools that run on their own. My first three years stayed within the first two levels. Asking a chatbot questions is convenient, but a chat window has no systematic way to handle work, and my tasks were growing bigger and running longer. Moving into the third level and beyond, at the end of my third year, was a natural next step. Moving the work out of the chat window In early June 2026 I watched a YouTube video demonstrating Codex, an AI agent shown printing shipping labels through a Telegram bot, and watching an inbox, summarizing new emails, and drafting replies. I asked Claude whether Claude Code could do the same. A search showed that the video overstated what Codex does, and the conversation turned into a different question: how would an ordinary user like me use this kind of AI? I felt uncomfortable pushing myself onto a new tool when I had no clear need for it and no clear understanding of it. Until then, I thought Claude Code was something developers used to write code, or to run several AI agents at once in separate windows. When I had asked about it in April, Claude had said much the same: it was meant for full-time developers. Still, I knew I would not learn it without trying it. There was no one I could ask about this in person, so on June 6 I sat down with Claude to work it out myself, starting with the characteristics of my work and what I needed. The repetitive part of my work that bothered me most turned out to be keeping track of commitments, such as when I had told a student I would get back to them, or what I had said would be on the next quiz. Those commitments were scattered across my journal, notes I sent to myself in a messaging app, Outlook, and things I said out loud in lectures, which were recorded on Zoom and transcribed. I rarely forgot them outright, but I often had the feeling that I was about to. We narrowed the plan to the two things my existing tools could not do: pull commitments out of lecture transcripts, and search my own saved notes by meaning. Reminders I could leave to my calendar. For storage I chose plain files in a Google Drive folder with an index, instead of Notion, so the records would not depend on an outside service or sit in my school account. To connect the pieces, Claude first suggested a workflow tool I had never heard of. When I asked whether that was what Claude Code was for, the plan shifted to Claude Code. I told Claude I did not really understand what Claude Code was, and installed it that day to try it. The first thing I asked it to do was read one of my lecture transcripts and list the promises I had made to students in class, such as "this will be on the next exam" or "I'll get to this next week." In 26 seconds it found fifteen, sorted them into categories, and pointed out which ones to deal with first. Then I asked it to save the list as a file, and it did. The same job in a chat window would have taken six steps on my part: open the file, copy the text, paste it into the chat, copy the answer, create a new file, and save it. In Claude Code it took two short requests, one for each. The AI behind both is the same, but the chat window can only answer, while Claude Code can also act on the files on my computer, asking my permission before each step. From that point on, I moved the work out of the chat window. That same day, the plan became the first version of the database described in the next section: a bot on the Mac mini that stays on, waits for messages from my phone, and files them. By the end of June, the research paper I was developing for the Math Readiness Initiative, with its analysis scripts and manuscript files, had moved to Claude Code as well.

Claude Code opens inside a folder on my computer. Each folder holds one kind of work along with everything that has been written down about it, and the agent reads those files before it does anything. Dividing the information this way lets each agent concentrate on its own role, working only from what it has been given. My college folder and my personal folder may both hold a schedule, for example, but the two schedules are about different things, and neither agent should confuse one with the other. I keep more than ten of these folders: some for the college, some personal, and some that exist for a single job, such as one piece of software. Course materials, lecture transcripts and lab notes One of these folders holds my teaching materials, built as a database. An agent read through my slides and wrote their content out as text files, organized by chapter and topic. It also linked the transcripts Zoom makes of my lecture recordings to the matching slides, so for any topic I can see both what the slides say and how I taught it in class. The folder holds my lab materials and the documents I have written for the college as well. During CHEM V120B last summer I sent field notes to it from the lab bench through the phone bot described above. Each recorded what went wrong with a procedure and what to change next time, written within minutes of seeing it. The lab technician's preparation emails and photos are there too, filed by course and by experiment in date order, so before a lab I can see how that experiment has been set up in past years. This semester the full-term section runs ahead of the late-start one, so after a full-term lecture an agent reads the Zoom transcript against my plan and drafts what to change when I teach that chapter to the late-start section. As the material grows, reading through all of it for every question stops working. An agent also analyzes new material as it comes in, so comparisons across semesters are ready when I need them, as with the list below. Recurring student difficulties I have taught CHEM V101 three times with recordings. The notes built from the Zoom transcripts of those three semesters list, chapter by chapter, the places where students got stuck, each tagged with how many of the three semesters it came up in. A place that came up once may come from something that happened that day. A place that came up in all three comes from the material itself, and students will likely get stuck there again. I read this list the evening before I teach a chapter, and it decided which of the simulations on the CHEM V101 Interactive Simulations page were built first.

The last of the levels in Getting Started with AI is where AI works directly with websites and services, instead of handing me text to carry over, and where I build tools that run on their own. In my work the service that matters most is Canvas, where every course at the college runs. The Canvas API Canvas is normally edited by clicking through its pages in a browser. It also has an API, a way for a program to reach a course directly without going through the screens. That lets my AI agent make changes for me. A change can be written down once as a script, a short set of instructions, and then run with one command however many pages it touches. I work this way in my own CHEM V101 courses, the chemistry department's shared course, and the Distance Education Advisory Group's course. Every change follows the same order: read what is there, run the change without saving it, show me the result, and only then write. A Canvas course for the Distance Education Advisory Group The Distance Education Advisory Group's working material was scattered. Older agendas and minutes sat on the college website, newer ones in a public board system that shows one meeting at a time, and the documents people shared during meetings lived in Teams chat threads. Answering "did we already discuss this?" meant knowing where to look and opening meetings one by one. I proposed a Canvas course for the group as its central repository. It came up at three meetings between March and May 2026, and in May the group supported it. Matthew Moore, one of the group's tri-chairs, created the shell that afternoon. I built the structure that evening, before any content went in. A Start Here module holds the group's charge, its roster and roles, its goals, its governance structure and the district's DE handbook. A Meetings module is organized by academic year. A Standing Items module mirrors the standing items on the group's own agenda: the DE strategic plan, AI and academic integrity, the testing center, accessibility. A Resource Library holds the rest. The meeting record went in once the frame was there, thirty-five meetings from September 2021 to May 2026 and sixty-eight documents. I gathered the older PDFs from the college website, and Claude Code sorted them by year and uploaded them. For the board system a script finds every published meeting, renders the agenda and minutes to PDF, and names them by date. Over the summer other members began adding to the course and editing its pages. The module list of the Distance Education Advisory Group's Canvas course: Start Here, Meetings, Standing Items, Resource Library, and AI-Use Showcase. The day the course was created I asked Matthew Moore to add Nectir, an AI assistant the college already had, and he installed it the next day. In June Meg Phelps, Instructional Technologist and Designer in Ventura College Distance Education, switched on its connection to Canvas at my request, and I configured it to answer from the group's own minutes and pages. At the first meeting of the fall, on September 10, the course was an agenda item. The group agreed without objection to enroll every member, and at a member's request I shared my screen and walked everyone through it. The next day Ali Olson-Pacheco, a member of the group, used Nectir to ask what work had already been done on revising the group's charge. It walked her through a year of minutes, and she found the working draft on the course's first page. I checked its answer against the minutes and corrected one line, because a pending clarification it had attached to the charge belonged to a different agenda item. Matthew Moore replied that the research would keep the group from reinventing the wheel. One academic year, 2024–25, is still missing from the course, the older files still carry their original names, and the sixteen PDFs the script rendered lack the accessibility tags the older, hand-made ones have. All three are on my list. The chemistry department's shared course The chemistry department keeps a shared Canvas course that works as a library for every chemistry instructor: syllabi, lab manuals, lecture materials, exams and videos for five courses. Over the years the files had piled up with no naming convention, the modules were organized in different ways, and old and current versions sat side by side, so an instructor opening it could not easily tell which version was current. I took on reorganizing it in July 2026. The CHEM V101 module in the chemistry department's shared Canvas course, listing six pages: Syllabus & Schedule, Lecture Materials, Lab Materials, Sample Tests, Sample Practice and Videos. Because the course belongs to the whole department, every bulk change went through the same steps. The agent first produced a table of what it would change, without changing anything, and I approved it. It then ran the change on one or two items and read them back from Canvas before the rest went ahead. Nothing was deleted: old versions were marked and hidden, and every change was logged so it can be undone. Each course now has the same six sections (Syllabus & Schedule, Lecture Materials, Lab Materials, Sample Tests, Sample Practice, Videos). Across the course, 398 files were renamed to one convention, the current V101 lab manual was uploaded (until then the course had held only the 2019 edition), and forty-three videos that had been stuck in unpublished modules were linked from new Videos pages. A "What Changed & When" page, generated from the log, lets colleagues find where their files went. In August, after I approved each batch, an agent added the markup a screen reader depends on to 140 table headers across forty pages, most of them pages the reorganization itself had created. The course also holds the department's meeting log, a summary page for each department meeting that I have kept since April 2025. There are eleven as of September 2026. One course in two Canvas shells Since Fall 2025, lecture and lab have been combined under one CRN, and Canvas creates a separate shell for each CRN, so a single course can end up split across several shells. The department has used two remedies: a blueprint, which copies one master shell into the others, and a hard link, which merges sections into one shell. I teach all of my late-start CHEM V101 sections, so I merged them into one shell. My two full-term sections could not be merged, because another instructor teaches one of the lab sections, so that course runs in two shells. After each class a summary has to go into both, in two parts: What Happened (the day's notes, the recording link, any quiz and its key) and What Will Happen (the next class, upcoming quizzes and deadlines). The day's files also have to be placed in the right module in each shell. I used to do all of that by hand, twice. Now one script does it for both shells. A Canvas announcement titled [9/23] Class Summary. Under What Happened: the Chapter 4 Day 1 notes, the recording link (hidden here), and Quiz 2 with its key. Under What Will Happen: finishing Chapter 4 with Practice Quiz 3 on Monday 9/28, Quiz 3 on Wednesday 9/30, a note on showing full setup in calculations, and the Chapter 4 Worksheet due 9/30.

The thirty-five simulations for CHEM V101 have a page of their own, CHEM V101 Interactive Simulations, which also describes how they were built. Comments matched to wrong answers on lab quizzes In September 2026 I began sending automatic comments on CHEM V101 lab quizzes, and have kept doing so since. Each wrong choice on a multiple-choice question has an explanation written in advance. After a quiz is graded, a script built with the agent puts together the explanations for the letters a student chose and posts them, with the graded scan, as a comment on that student's submission. It works when a quiz is entirely multiple choice; free-response work is still graded by hand. A classroom clock and timer Once the simulations were working, I wondered whether I could make a clock as well. I put a timer on the projector whenever the class is working against time, such as a quiz or fifteen minutes on a practice set. The free clock site I had been using had filled with advertising, which is a distraction in front of a class during a quiz. So I made my own (tools.rubyeye19.com/clock). It is a single HTML file with no external dependencies, a clock and a countdown timer readable from the back of the room. Because nothing loads from outside, it keeps working if the network drops mid-class. An empty lecture hall photographed from the back row. The projector screen at the front shows the clock, 2:22:33 PM, with the date Monday, September 28, 2026 beneath it. The digits are legible from the last row of seats. The same projector screen showing the countdown timer at 19:57, with a thin progress bar running across the screen below the digits. The same site also holds a map of places to eat around Oxnard and Ventura (tools.rubyeye19.com/eats). In October 2026 I put it in the orientation module of my three Canvas courses and asked students to recommend places they like. A recommendation comes in through a form, and I review it before it goes on the map. Students recommended nine different places in the first two days. On October 20, 2026 I put the map on the projector during lecture and students talked through which of the places they would recommend. By the afternoon of October 21 the map held thirty places, twenty-nine of them recommended by students. The Oxnard & Ventura Eats page on October 21, 2026: the recommendation list on the left, sorted by most recommended, and thirty pins on the map from Ojai to Agoura Hills, most of them around Ventura, Oxnard and Camarillo. Twenty-nine of the places were recommended by students. The names in the list are the nicknames students chose; one that could be a real name is covered. Map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors. Next steps Until now I have brought AI into my work in the same order each time, starting from something that was missing and then finding a tool to fill it, as with keeping track of what I had promised students or posting the same class summary to two Canvas shells. That order made sense while I understood my own work far better than I understood the tools, and adopting a tool I neither needed nor understood would have been a risk. My understanding of the tools has since caught up with my understanding of the work, so I can start from an idea as well as from a problem. The simulations are one example. They started from something I wanted, which was to give students a wider range of things to try and practice, and having them inside Canvas would make my hybrid section more fully a hybrid course. Building them would have been far out of reach if AI were not writing the code, and once it was, it became a matter of deciding to try. The next step is to keep trying ideas I would once have set aside, and to check each one before it reaches a student, as I did with the simulations.
