t: CHEM V101 Lab Manual Renewal Project
x: Origin When I began teaching CHEM V101 (formerly V20L), the lab manual worked well. Teaching from it week after week, though, I kept noticing small things I wished were different, and they added up. For example: Each lab used its own headings and its own section order. Some combined background and procedure; others split them across pages. Instructions switched between commands and passive description with no pattern. Equations were saved as images, so they could not be reused or displayed cleanly in Canvas. Sample calculations sat inside paragraphs instead of being set out as worked examples. The manual could still be taught as it was, but the list kept growing, so in Summer 2025 I decided to update the manual myself. First revision, Summer 2025 The revision had two goals, consistency and readability. There was no editable source file for the manual, so I retyped every lab from the existing copy. The main changes: Same structure in every lab. Each one follows the same sections in the same order: Background, Procedure, Data, Post-Lab. Numbered steps. Paragraph instructions became numbered steps, each starting with an action verb (Measure, Record, Mix). Shorter background. Background text was cut to what students need for that lab. Clearer data tables. Tables were given more visual weight, so a new sample is visibly a new sample. Safety where it can be seen. Safety points that used to be buried mid-sentence moved into shaded Note and Caution boxes. In July I sent the proposed direction to Erin Brocker and Kristin Clark, with Antonia Flores copied. Kristin pushed back on a two-column procedure layout, because students need one spaced-out column they can follow and check off. Erin agreed, for accessibility, and I kept the procedure in a single column. Erin also suggested Tahoma for the body text, because it keeps capital I, lowercase l and the numeral 1 distinct, which matters when students read Cl and NaCl. I had planned to use Calibri and switched. Antonia went through the labs for content while I worked on format. I would have liked to lay the manual out in InDesign, but I built it in Word, because the manual has to stay editable by other instructors and they could not have opened an InDesign file. All the labs were compiled into one formatted document and distributed through Canvas before Fall 2025. Fall 2025 in use The revised manual went into classrooms, and problems surfaced that the summer edit had not caught. I had simplified the procedures, which changed the step numbers. To keep the changes small I had left the Pre-Lab and Post-Lab questions as they were, so questions that pointed to a procedure step by number now pointed to the wrong step. Erin Brocker caught this. Step numbering also drifted between labs (one lab began at step 24), and there were typos, inconsistent table captions, and missing units in worked examples. Because all the labs had been revised in a single round, patching them created new inconsistencies as fast as it fixed old ones. Erin suggested going back to the previous version, and I agreed. On September 29, 2025, I wrote to the CHEM V101 instructors that the revised manual was withdrawn for now, shared the previous version through the department's Canvas course, and said I would fix the revision and check it with them before releasing it again. I apologized for the disruption and offered two ways to give feedback: printed copies to mark up or a shared document to edit directly. The failure was mine, and my colleagues saw it in the middle of a semester. Second revision, Summer 2026 Over the winter I decided to stop patching, set up a process that prevents the Fall 2025 failure, and then re-author the manual under it. In April 2026 I turned the manual's background and procedure sections into Canvas pages, with videos linked to the procedure steps, and asked the department's instructors to review that version. The videos are described on the CHEM V101 Experiment Video Reference Library page. Diagnosis first. Before writing anything I compared the current printed manual and the failed revision one to one across all seventeen experiments, and recorded a verdict for each experiment in a table. The comparison found nine defects that ran through the whole manual. The first was the Fall 2025 problem: Pre-Lab and Post-Lab questions referred to steps by number ("steps 6–9", "Question N") that no longer matched the procedure, and in some labs the steps they named no longer existed. The audit also found problems that had nothing to do with formatting: A copy-pasted waste-disposal line, "no hazardous material, may be drained to the sink", sat in a barium experiment. That is a safety defect. A missing UV blindness warning, and a missing hot-plate burn warning, both restored. A specific heat mistyped as 0.131 instead of 0.191, plus an arithmetic error in the same worked example. A worked example that contradicted the actual composition of the compound it described. Copyrighted material from a commercial supplier in one experiment, and an unlicensed photograph from the web in another, both removed and replaced with diagrams drawn in house. A flame test with a history of not reproducing in the actual lab. I removed it and reorganized the experiment around precipitation-based identification. A background section describing a pH meter the experiment does not use. Build system. A shared style module defines the caution badges, the chemical-formula helper, the answer boxes and the two-column calculation layout. Scripts generate each experiment, and an assembler produces the table of contents, global page numbers, PDF bookmarks, and the odd-page section starts the print run requires. The manual can be rebuilt from its source files at any time. Each experiment was saved as its own commit (a recorded version with a note explaining the change), so the revision history is the audit trail. I settled two design decisions by building the options and comparing them: two full design samples, and five body fonts typeset onto the same page. Answer keys as verification. I wrote all thirty-four answer keys myself, because working every solution is how I find out whether every question can be answered. The student manual is 218 pages, with seventeen experiments, six appendices and front matter. It includes the re-typeset safety rules, an equipment poster, and a calculator appendix rendered in the keycap notation from the device's own guide, so a student can follow the buttons visually. Review copy for colleagues, with change notes The review copy is a separate 277-page document built to draw specific feedback. Each experiment opens with a table comparing the current version with the proposed one (item, what changed, why). I wrote the tables by checking all seventeen experiments page by page against the actual old manual, because a table is only useful to a reviewer if it is exact. After the table comes a checkpoint sheet listing real reagent concentrations and volumes for the reviewer to confirm, with safety and timing checks, then the lab body, then the answer keys, which show that every question can be answered. Three review rounds preceded it, including a cold usability review of my own build. That review found a design flaw: the safety agreement's keep-copy and submit-copy were printed on two sides of a single sheet, so a student submitting it gave up the copy they were told to keep. Review copy, Experiment 1 chapter cover: each change from the current manual listed with what changed and why, followed by the tips and cautions that are new. Review copy, Experiment 1 checkpoint sheet: reagent concentrations for the reviewer to confirm against the stockroom, plus checks on timing, safety and whether the questions still match the procedure. Printed review copies went to colleagues on August 7, 2026. A lab technician copy was designed separately, as a short checklist of reagent and equipment values to confirm at the bench. The department's revised safety rules (forty rules reduced to eighteen, effective in spring) arrived mid-project. I applied them right away. Moving to LibreTexts and an open license Until August 2026 the manual was a set of Word files built from scripts that only I ran. In August I wrote to the campus LibreTexts contact about moving it into LibreTexts, where instructors can work on one shared copy, and asked to coordinate with the CHEM V104 effort already under way. On August 27 the seventeen experiments and six appendices went into a private LibreTexts book. The pages are generated from the same source files as the printed manual, so the manual can be revised and moved at the same time. Each experiment page also carries its videos. The same day I wrote to the department about the book and invited colleagues into it. At the department's lab safety meeting on September 18, 2026, Erin Brocker proposed that each instructor take experiments and work on them individually. On September 20 I opened a workspace for that in the department's Canvas course, one discussion with a reply for each of the seventeen experiments, each linked to its LibreTexts draft, and announced it to the department's instructors. Kristin Clark took Experiments 8 and 12, and Crystal Serrano took Experiments 9 and 10. On October 5 Erin posted her own versions of eleven experiments, and I compared each with the current draft and replied in the thread. Antonia Flores answered the stockroom questions those comparisons raised, and her answers went into the manual (the silver nitrate in Experiment 8, for example, is 0.1 M). On September 29 I asked the department which open license to build to, and on October 10 we settled on CC BY-NC-SA. The October 10 message also carried a review form that collects the questions still open from the October 5 comparisons, forty-two questions in seventeen sections. The manual is free to students: it is printed through the campus copy center and given away. Without an open license or a shared repository yet, it counts as zero-textbook-cost. Once it is published under CC BY-NC-SA, it will also be OER. The department now plans a Fall 2027 launch, moving most or all of its lab manuals to LibreTexts together.

t: CHEM V101 Experiment Video Reference Library
x: The CHEM V104 videos The V101 library grew out of an earlier project. In Fall 2024 Antonia Flores had a CHEM V104 student who is hearing-impaired and attended lab with a sign-language interpreter, and she asked whether captioned videos of each experiment could let the student preview the lab. Antonia performed and narrated each experiment; I filmed, edited and captioned them, with captions aligned by hand. By Summer 2025 the full V104 set was published on the Ventura College Chemistry YouTube channel and in Canvas, and the work was paid through a district stipend posted for the chemistry lab video project. (The full story is on the CHEM V104 Laboratory Demo Video Project page.) Those were instructional videos: a narrated walk through each lab, meant to be watched before coming in. The V101 recording run After the V104 series was finished, I turned to CHEM V101, recording all twelve experiments on the regular semester schedule between January and April 2026. That took about fifteen hours of recording, then roughly eleven hours of editing and two hours of Canvas work. The output is 67 videos, 20 photographs, and 13 Canvas pages, published to the Ventura College Chemistry YouTube channel and embedded into the online lab manual on Canvas. Close-up reference clips For V101 I wanted something different from the V104 videos. Instead of narrated instruction, these are close-up reference clips: short, minimally edited, no audio, showing the detail a student cannot see from the back of the room. They sit inside the online lab manual next to the step they show, as a supplement to the instructor's own pre-lab talk. A student who wants to see exactly how a meniscus is read can scrub a short clip frame by frame without hunting for the moment inside a longer narrated video. Making it a department resource The V104 videos became a department resource through the stipend: paid work, published through YouTube and Canvas for any instructor to use. The V101 clips were made outside that arrangement. To come under the same model, the V101 clips need closed captions added, because a stipend-funded library is held to the accessibility standard of the V104 set. That update is what I am preparing now, and I have asked the department how to open a stipend for it. Next steps The recording is done. The caption update comes next, once the stipend question is settled. I would like to build the same kind of library for CHEM V120B. The timing is not set.

t: CHEM V104 Laboratory Demo Video Project
x: Background and purpose CHEM V104 combines general and organic chemistry at a faster pace than the introductory sequence, and many students meet a chemistry lab for the first time in it. The course was numbered V30L when this was made. I had wanted to build a video archive of the lab sequence, but how it would be used was still open. I had worked with video before I came to the college, and in the summer of 2024 Antonia Flores and I had finished the lab safety video series together. In Fall 2024 one of Antonia's V104 sections included a student who is hearing-impaired and attended with a sign-language interpreter. Live lab demonstrations move quickly and happen over background noise, and the interpreter found it hard to translate every step in real time. Antonia suggested that the student preview each experiment on video before the session. That case settled how the archive would be used: as a shared teaching resource, built to be accessible and organized so that other instructors could use it in their own sections. Production Antonia set the schedule, two days after she raised the idea. It ran one lab a week, each recorded the week before that lab met, in the room the lab is taught in. Experiment 5 was left out because it covers nomenclature and Lewis structures and has no bench work to record, and the experiments V104 shares with the introductory lab were marked so we could tell which videos would be reused. The schedule followed the course, so the person teaching the course wrote it. From there the work divided along the same line. Antonia decided what a video needed to show, prepared the setups and reagents, made the procedure slides, and checked every cut for procedural and terminological accuracy. I ran the camera, the edit, the captions, and the distribution. Where I had something to add it was usually about what the camera could carry: which reactions to record for an experiment students rarely get to watch closely, or putting a thermometer in the shot so a temperature change is visible rather than narrated. Antonia's notes were exact. She would give a caption for a clip second by second, or ask for one segment to be moved behind another, and at first she was sending them as screenshots pasted into email, which meant I had to match her picture back to a point in the timeline. Since the rough cuts were already uploaded for her to watch, I asked her to leave the notes as comments on the videos themselves, where every comment carries the timestamp it was written at. The review moved there and stayed there. Reshoots were requested the same way, and one video was added at the end of the run because she wanted the volumetric pipette handled on its own. The result was 41 videos, captioned, delivered as standalone tutorials, so a single technique can be assigned on its own. Use and reach By Summer 2025 the full set was complete and published in three places: an unlisted playlist on the Ventura College Chemistry YouTube channel, uploads to Canvas Studio linked directly in course modules for both lecture and lab sections, and a shared folder on the department Canvas page so other faculty could embed or download. Unlisted means the videos are open to anyone given the link, which is everyone who uses them, without turning up in search. I created the channel for the department and gave Antonia admin access to it. The videos were placed where a student would meet them before the lab, as the original request asked. Because the files were captioned, clearly labeled, and modular, any section could use them without reformatting. Reflection The filming ran on the schedule set at the start. The dates in that first timeline are the dates we shot on, week after week, through a full teaching term, and the pace was light enough that neither Antonia nor I was carrying it on top of everything else. The part that ran long was the paperwork: the videos were finished and in use well before the stipend they were done under was written and posted, and the agreement for the work was still being routed a year after the last video went up. The project also gave me a use for something I had set aside. I am not trained in media, but I have had a lot of chances to work on it, for a friend's media company and at my church, and none of it had ever been for a school. I was glad to bring that experience to the department.

t: CHEM V101 Lecture Demonstration — Limiting Reactant Visualization
x: Overview This short in-class demonstration was used to visualize the concept of limiting reactants during the Stoichiometry and Gas Laws lecture. Students often find the limiting reagent abstract when discussed purely as a calculation problem; this visual setup allowed them to observe how gas production stops once one reactant is consumed, even when the other remains in excess. Three 125 mL Erlenmeyer flasks were prepared with equal amounts of 1 M HCl (20 mL each) and varying masses of NaHCO₃ (1 g, 2 g, and 3 g). Balloons were fitted on top of each flask to collect the CO₂ gas produced. The different balloon sizes showed the reaction yield, which is set by whichever reactant runs out first (the limiting reactant). Teaching purpose While the reaction proceeded, students predicted which reactant would limit CO₂ formation, performed mole-ratio calculations, and compared their theoretical results with the observed balloon volumes. The demonstration was built around three ideas: The limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield. Adding excess of the other reactant does not increase product formation once the limit is reached. Stoichiometric reasoning can be directly connected to visual and quantitative data. Three 125 mL flasks of hydrochloric acid, each capped with a balloon. The balloon on the 1 g flask is small; the balloons on the 2 g and 3 g flasks are inflated to the same size. The same three flasks with labels added: carbon dioxide at the top with CO₂ molecules drawn inside the inflated balloon, baking soda at left, hydrochloric acid at right. Animation of the three flasks as the reaction runs, the balloons rising from flat to inflated. Procedure and result Each flask contained 20 mL of 1 M HCl solution, while the baking soda (NaHCO₃) was measured and placed inside the balloon before attaching it to the flask. When the balloon was lifted, the powder fell into the acid, immediately generating bubbles of CO₂ gas that inflated the balloon. In the first two samples, increasing the mass of NaHCO₃ caused visibly larger balloons, and students could see that more reactant produced more gas. However, by the third flask (~3 g NaHCO₃), the balloon was no bigger than the second in any way you could see. More solid was present, but the reaction stopped once all available HCl had been consumed. This identified the acid as the limiting reactant. Past a certain point, adding more of one substance no longer increases the yield, because the other reactant is completely used up. Reaction and stoichiometry NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ — 1 mol NaHCO₃ → 1 mol CO₂ Sample NaHCO₃ (g) mol NaHCO₃ mol HCl Limiting reagent mol CO₂ Volume CO₂ @ STP (22.4 L mol⁻¹) #1 1.00 0.0119 0.020 NaHCO₃ 0.0119 0.0119 × 22.4 = 0.267 L (267 mL) #2 2.00 0.0238 0.020 HCl 0.0200 0.0200 × 22.4 = 0.448 L (448 mL) #3 3.00 0.0357 0.020 HCl 0.0200 0.0200 × 22.4 = 0.448 L (448 mL) Conclusions It ran on October 9, 2025, in a class Joe Selzler was observing. Two weeks earlier the written feedback from Jeffrey Wood's observation had recommended bringing live demonstrations into lecture, and Joe had suggested the same in conversation and lent me his books of demonstrations. His written record of the October 9 class notes the demonstration as a strength and asks that the discussion afterward run longer. My own read was less generous. The preparation happened before class and took longer than the demonstration itself did, and stopping to run it broke the flow of a lecture built around slides I annotate as I go. The balloons were also a coarse instrument for the thing I most needed them to show: the difference between the second flask and the third is the lesson, and it is the difference two inflated balloons show least well. What did read clearly from across the room was the part students already expected — more baking soda, more gas. That cause and effect was so obvious that it drew attention away from the mechanism underneath it. By the end of it I thought that running this in every section, every term, might be more than it gives back. It also made me settle how I divide lab and lecture. In my courses chemical demonstrations belong to lab, where the bench, the preparation time, and students standing close enough to watch are all part of the room, and in lecture I want the time to go to the lecture content. I still wanted to show more in lecture, and I kept asking how. What I arrived at was a simulation. It appears in the minute the calculation is happening, costs nothing to set up, and can run in every section and every term. The limiting reactant is one of the pieces in it, the same idea as these three flasks with the balloons replaced by two bars that drain at the rate the coefficients set and stop when one of them reaches the floor. It is documented in CHEM V101 Interactive Simulations.

Summer 2024 · Faculty Special Project Stipend, Office of Academic Affairs Objective The goal of the project was a safety video made for the Chemistry Department at Ventura College and its own lab safety procedures, so that safety instruction is more relevant and students engage with and remember the protocols. Rather than a long, generic safety film of the kind organizations such as the American Chemical Society publish, the video breaks the department's own safety checklist into short scenes matched to what students will do in our labs. The department had tried this before I arrived. The plan then was to make the videos with CAPS, the local community media organization, and it did not finish: the arrangement covered filming but not the editing without further cost, and what had been shot was not good enough to use. Six rough cuts from February 2019 survive, one per technique. The fire blanket scene is the clearest case: the person wraps the blanket around themselves standing up and walks out of frame, and the clip ends there, fourteen seconds long, without the part where you get down on the floor. When I mentioned in my interview that I had done video work, a video the department could make in house became possible, and the request came to me. The work was funded as a Faculty Special Project Stipend for Summer 2024 and carried out with Antonia Flores, with laboratory technician Kai Liang supporting the filming. Development Planning. In April 2024 I wrote to the department's faculty with the plan and its stages, showed example video styles, and asked which safety procedures to include and what format would fit their teaching. I drew the storyboard; Antonia Flores and Kai Liang reviewed it slide by slide, and at the end of May the revised version went to the department with a three-day shooting plan. Preparation. I set the scenes for each shooting day and how many student workers each needed, and Antonia and Kai arranged the dates with the student workers. I sent out the attire for the safe and unsafe examples, which they passed on to the student workers, and I set up the equipment on each shooting day. Filming. Three sessions of roughly two hours each, covering scenarios such as using an eyewash station, handling chemicals, and appropriate lab attire. Editing and post-production. Footage was processed in stages with departmental feedback at each step; the edit was brought to visual consistency with color grading, and closed-captioned for accessibility. Several versions were produced (with and without background music, combined and segmented) in MP4, GIF, and PowerPoint with embedded GIFs, for flexibility in how it is shown. Feedback and refinement. Clip order, captions, and graphics were revised on departmental input. Final product and implementation The completed video is a visual guide to common lab safety mistakes and best practice, in three forms: one for in-class presentation, one for on-demand viewing on Canvas, and a segmented version that can be attached to individual lab sessions. I show it on the first day of class, colleagues have shown it in their own sections, and it remains available on Canvas for reference throughout the term. Challenges Lighting consistency. The shooting window was short, and the lighting could not be reset for every scene, so color varied between shots. It was corrected in grading. Timeline. The project ran alongside a summer teaching assignment, so editing was prioritized to finish before the fall semester. Distribution and follow-up projects The video was posted to the chemistry department's Canvas so that any instructor can copy it into their own course, which is how it reached sections other than mine. I have also been told, in conversation, that departments outside chemistry have used it. Discussions with faculty and administrators at the time pointed to next steps: additional videos on specific techniques and equipment handling; versions that students working with interpreters can review at their own pace; a pre-lab video series for the laboratory courses ahead of the college's move to a compressed calendar; and collaboration with other departments whose labs could use the same approach. Several of these have since happened: the CHEM V104 and V101 video libraries continue this project.

Overview A library of interactive simulations for CHEM V101, thirty-five as of September 2026, published in the course's Canvas modules. Each simulation is a single HTML file. A student clicks a link in a module and it runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account to create. Three of the simulations as a student first sees them: Limiting Reactant with two reactant columns and the smaller product amount chosen, Mole Map with grams of AgNO₃ given and grams of AgCl to solve for, and the start screen of the Naming Speed Run. Goals Show on screen what I used to explain in words. In lecture I explain a lot through analogies. For electronegativity, I describe a crowd on a street drifting toward the more famous person. The Electronegativity difference simulation shows that analogy on screen. A student picks two elements, and the electron cloud slides toward the more electronegative atom. The Electronegativity Difference simulation with H and Cl selected: the difference of 0.9 falls in the polar covalent band, and the shared electron cloud carries δ+ on H and δ− on Cl. The limiting-reactant simulation carries the same idea as the flasks and balloons on the CHEM V101 Lecture Demonstration page, with the balloons replaced by two bars that drain at the rate the coefficients set. Give students in the hybrid section more to do in Canvas. Most of a Canvas course is pages to read and files to upload. The naming speed game, for example, is a timed round of ten compounds that a student can play alone at home. Content from my lectures Examples I use in class. Students can work through the same examples they saw on my slides and in my lecture notes. Balancing by counting uses the equations from my slides. The coefficients move, the subscripts stay locked, and a table counts the atoms on each side. Unit conversion chain reproduces the worked examples from my notes. Dilution reproduces the problems from my notes. Points I return to in class. My lectures are recorded, and the record of three runs of this course shows which points I make every term. X in the denominator covers solving for a variable in the denominator, which comes up in density, molar mass and the gas laws. Calculator keystrokes covers entering scientific notation with parentheses or the EE key. Mole ratio is not mass ratio covers converting grams to moles before applying the ratio. Every number in the simulations was checked against my lecture notes. How they were built I wanted demonstrations that fit lecture, and more in Canvas for students to do than read pages and upload files. Building them used to be out of reach, because I would have had to learn to program first. The database described on the Teaching Materials Database page is what made them possible. I did not have to explain my course, because the agent already had the analogy I use for electronegativity, the numbers I put on the board and the order I teach topics in, so what students open in Canvas matches what they heard in lecture. Through the API, each simulation goes onto the module page next to the material it belongs to, and a fix is re-uploaded to every course that uses it in one run. There are thirty-five as of September 2026. Each one still goes past me before students see it. One showed a rearranged equation with a ÷ sign, and I had it rebuilt as a fraction, because the point of that lesson is that x is in the denominator and a ÷ sign hides it. Use in Canvas Each simulation opens on the module page, next to the material it belongs to. A student enters a value, moves a slider or drags a piece, and the screen responds. When a step is wrong, the simulation refuses it and shows the reason. Sharing When an instructor copies the Canvas page into another course, the simulation comes with it and works there. Any instructor who wants one can take it. Status All thirty-five are published in the course modules. I have asked students to tell me which simulations they would like, and I add new ones for lecture and lab as ideas come up. In Fall 2024 I served as a peer evaluator for an adjunct instructor teaching CHEM V20 (now V101), Elementary Chemistry. The observation was part of the district's regular adjunct faculty evaluation process under Form A2, with Dean Aaron Jones and Chair Malia Rose-Seisa on the committee. My role was to observe one lecture, submit a written evaluation, and contribute to the committee's final summary. The session covered limiting reactants and percent yield. The instructor worked each calculation step by step on the Docucam and used a cheesecake recipe as an analogy for percent yield. The tone was supportive and approachable throughout. Observation summary Focus area Observation Suggestion Docucam Calculations worked step by step on the Docucam helped students follow. Lower the brightness; it was too bright to read comfortably. Questioning Sequential questions to individual students kept the class engaged and added time to the lesson. — Calculations by hand Working each calculation by hand rather than with a calculator sometimes interrupted the flow. Prepare calculation steps in advance, and use a calculator for some steps. Examples The cheesecake analogy made percent yield relatable. — Committee review I attended the committee's final evaluation meeting on November 12, 2024, submitted my Form A2 that day, and signed the committee's summary evaluation (Form C1) on December 9.

Purpose We turned an underused hallway display case on the third floor of the Science Building into a Chemistry faculty introduction board to improve visibility, student–faculty connection, and departmental identity. The goal was a board that is clean, durable, and easy to update, showing each instructor's profile alongside quick-access links for students. My role I was the design and implementation lead from concept through print production, and I kept faculty, lab staff, and the division lead informed along the way. That meant drafting the initial concept and presenting prototypes for group feedback; reconciling several style preferences through iterative samples; building and running a Google Form to collect bios and photos; scheduling a photo session for those who wanted professional consistency; monitoring submissions and adapting when the form malfunctioned by accepting email responses instead; testing multiple print vendors to compare color accuracy, finish, and cost; and documenting changes and approvals so the decisions stayed traceable. The division lead defined the content fields, oversaw branding, and approved the final purchase; a lab technician assisted with reminders, vendor research, and installation; faculty contributors supplied bios and photos and reviewed proofs. The board Profile card system — modular tiles on a consistent grid, with a shared icon set and a QR code. Information set — name, office, email, a short "about me," education, interests, plus an optional specialty tag and role label. Scalable layout — cards designed at 9 × 9 in and planned as a 4 × 4 array for sixteen profiles, later redesigned at 9 × 10 in for readability, with alternating left/right blocks. Each card is printed scaled to fit a letter-size sheet. At installation I arranged the cards to fit the display case, and later rearranged them three across in each door. Wayfinding and updates — QR links to the division and faculty pages; outer acrylic holders for rotating event flyers. Seven prototype versions of one profile card, from a plain layout with the college logo to a dark full-bleed design, made for the group's feedback before the template was settled. Process Seven prototypes were produced, from minimal to more decorative, with icons and branding restored per feedback and position labels added. Data came in through a structured Google Form with word limits, backed by reminders and scheduled photo sessions. For print, we compared copy-center and FedEx output and tested gloss against matte, landing on 100-lb matte cardstock for clarity and tone balance. Feedback through the review rounds was consistent (readable font, softer background, professional but friendly), and the division authorized the purchase once the files were resized and finalized. The cards were built in InDesign and the images prepared in Photoshop. The layout is a frame-based template: each card is a set of fixed frames, so a new photo drops into place. With twelve profiles arriving at different times and in different formats, that is what made the set practical to assemble and, later, to add to. Design rationale Legibility came first, so the type is enlarged, the contrast is balanced, and the spacing is generous. Icons make the card quick to scan, and the QR code replaces text that would otherwise clutter it. The modular layout means future additions and replacements need no redesign. The VC logo, a chemistry color palette, and unified typography give the department a visual identity in the building. Maintenance The update workflow is deliberately short: faculty submit through the form or by email, the template is updated, cards are batch-printed, and the installed set is swapped. External acrylic holders carry announcements and division flyers, and the QR codes link to the department's official pages. In fall 2026 the board took three new cards, for part-time instructors who joined the department this semester: one early in the term and two more on September 29, each collected through the same Google Form and built from the existing template. It now holds fifteen profiles. The planned layout, a mockup with sample profiles: sixteen cards in a 4 × 4 array across the two doors of the display case. The board as first installed, in place by January 2026: twelve profile cards, with the chair's card under the header and element tiles along the top of the right door. The rearranged layout, in place by February 2026, photographed September 28, 2026 after a thirteenth card was added: cards three across in each door. The board on September 29, 2026, with two more cards added: fifteen profiles across the two doors. Reflection Before Ventura College I spent several years on staff at a church in Orange County, a few of them leading its media team. That work was posters, slide decks, event graphics, and printed programs, designed on a deadline for a group of people who all had opinions about it. I did not expect it to come up again in a chemistry department, and it turned out to be the part of my background this project drew on most. Coordinating among faculty meant balancing preferences that are easy to underestimate: how each person wanted to be represented, how formal the tone should be, how much visual personality to include. Reconciling those took the same thing it took at the church: showing samples instead of describing options, iterating, following up. The project was shaped by small steps: testing a print sample, revising a layout after feedback, adjusting the form so others could join more easily. I would like to keep using that experience here.

Purpose Ventura College's Zero Textbook Cost and ZEN initiatives exist to remove financial barriers to learning. Within that framework I converted CHEM V101, lecture and lab, as part of the Pre-Allied Health Pathway Acceleration Grant. The course serves pre-nursing and allied-health students. General chemistry textbooks commonly list above $250 when bundled with a lab manual, and a national survey has found that most college students have skipped buying a required text because of cost. Converting the course addressed that directly, and it also rebuilt how students reach and move through the chemistry materials. Before the conversion CHEM V101 was already close to zero cost before the ZEN program, though I had not measured it against the formal criteria. Lectures ran on slides I wrote, homework on worksheets I wrote, and the lab manual was a free PDF students could work in digitally, print themselves, or open on the lab computers, with printed copies available on request. The syllabus still listed a commercial text, because that is what the course's official materials list said, and in class I told students not to buy it and pointed them to a free online one instead. So the course was already free in practice while the paperwork still said otherwise, and a student reading the syllabus before the first day had no way to know that. The course lacked the structure that makes a free course usable: materials in the order they are needed, a lecture and a lab that point at each other, and a license that lets anyone else take the work. The conversion Canvas rebuilt as weekly modules. The course had been a flat archive of files. It became weekly units, each carrying its readings, slides, guided worksheets, quizzes, and recorded lectures with searchable transcripts, so a student meets materials in the order the week uses them. Lecture and lab aligned. The two halves were brought into the same sequence, so what a week covers in lecture is what that week's lab does. Textbook adoption made formal. The free text I had been pointing students to became the course's listed one (LibreTexts for CHEM V101, OpenStax for CHEM V120B), so the course's zero-cost status rests on an adoption on the record rather than on what I say in the room. Lab manual revised alongside the lecture materials, for less printing and better use on a screen. That document has since gone through a failed release, a rollback, and a full re-authoring, described on the CHEM V101 Lab Manual Renewal Project page. Paid homework tools examined. I started looking for a free platform that could replace them, which is work that continued past this project and is written up under Tools I Tried. Collaboration ran throughout, with the ZEN team, the Life Sciences department, and the Distance Education Advisory Group, to keep ADA compliance, copyright safety, and Canvas integration consistent across STEM courses. Scope and results The ZEN committee selected the course for conversion on Pathway One (original content curation and creation), the larger of the two tracks offered that term. It ran as a district special project from January 27 to May 2, 2025, sized at 81–120 hours, with completion verified that May. All materials are freely available to students and openly licensed where applicable. What the work left behind is the course's weekly-module structure, which the shared CHEM V101 Canvas shell has used since Fall 2025 (see Linked Lecture–Lab Coordination). The conversion also fed the college's ZTC Acceleration Grant data reporting, documenting Chemistry's readiness within the Pre-Allied Health pathway. I learned curriculum design, transfer policy, and narrative compliance on this project, and I have used them since in the ZTC and OER sequencing work.

Project S:AIL in STEM (Servingness: Aspiration, Identity, and Learning) was Ventura College's Title III HSI STEM grant project. In Fall 2024 it ran a professional development series for early-career and adjunct STEM faculty, on equity-informed pedagogy and on navigating tenure inside a Hispanic-Serving Institution. Facilitated by Adrienne Arguijo, Gema Espinoza Sanchez, and Dr. Raeanne Napoleon, the series combined weekly coaching, guided reflection, and collaborative discussion across five sessions, four in person and one asynchronous. Session 1 (November 1) — The Students. Cultural introductions and affective coaching practices in STEM classrooms. Participants reflected on their own cultural identities, teaching personas, and early-career paths, guided by discussion of discomfort as a catalyst for learning and of "stepping up / stepping back" as a facilitation tool. Session 2 (November 8) — Pedagogy and Practice I. An asynchronous module on race-conscious pedagogy: Dr. Christopher Emdin on teaching identity and classroom authenticity, Dr. Roni Ellington's AAAS talk on culturally responsive teaching in STEM, and readings from Dr. Gina Ann Garcia's Transforming HSIs for Equity and Justice. The work was journaling and Padlet reflection on the question of who I am as a teacher in this space. Session 3 (November 15) — Pedagogy and Practice II. This session combined data inquiry with equity-minded storytelling. Counterstories: Transforming the Narrative Through Data Inquiry introduced ways to read institutional data through lived experience rather than deficit models, and the HSI Summit presentation connected that to the college's own master plan goals. The practical exercise was reframing data as community stories, so that the causes identified are institutional rather than student-based. Session 4 (November 22) — Roundtable. A brunch roundtable combining pedagogical application with career preparation: STEM academic counseling integrated into courses, a syllabus-as-a-tool-for-racial-equity activity using the USC Race & Equity Center review guide, and a roundtable with faculty and deans on CVs, cover letters, teaching demonstrations, and tenure navigation. Session 5 (December 6) — The Self. The closing workshop returned to syllabus redesign, finishing equity-centered syllabi grounded in inclusive tone and transparent expectations. The discussion on sustaining change treated discomfort, reflection, and collaboration as ongoing work.

Professional Development · Distance Education Advisory Group I am reworking my CHEM V101 lecture slides into an open textbook on LibreTexts, with newly drawn figures and fuller explanations, and plan to do most of the work over the 2026–27 winter break. Three chapters are complete and a fourth is in progress as of October 20, 2026. The sample chapter went to department colleagues for comment and to my students in the week it was taught. Student participation in lecture The observers' requests. Last fall's observation reports ask for more structured interaction between students during lecture. The specifics were wait time after a question, repeating student answers aloud and using names, and Think-Pair-Share. The reports themselves are on the Committee Observation Feedback page. Status of each request. Wait time after a question is part of how I run lecture now. Peer explanation is built into this fall's CHEM V101 lectures as a short peer teach-back: while working a problem, students explain a step aloud to a partner, in the chapters where explaining carries the concept. I designed it over the summer as part of the Math Readiness work, for the fluent student who learns most by explaining, and it is the kind of peer interaction the observers had asked for. In practice it has settled at the moment a practice block opens, and it has yet to show up inside an explanation. This fall's feedback reminded me to repeat student answers aloud. I went back through the transcripts of this fall's lectures to see how often I was doing it, and found it in every recorded lecture in both sections. The feedback had caught something narrower, which is that a quiet answer can reach me and still be lost to the rest of the room, and I now make sure those are heard. The same transcripts show that I rarely use students' names, and that is the part I have yet to make a habit. For students who would rather not answer in front of the room, I tell them they can signal me with a look, the way people bid at an auction, and I read those signals as I go. The document camera. Sharing student work on the document camera was a colleague's suggestion after an observation in Fall 2025. I tried it in lecture that October, with two correct solutions and one incorrect one side by side, and the observer that day found that the comparison made the concept clearer. It also put one student's error in front of the whole room, which I was uneasy about, and it interrupted the way I normally run a problem session. I have stopped showing an individual student's work. I already know which mistakes come up most often, so I point those out during lecture, and no one in the room has to be the example. In the peer teach-back a student's error is heard by one partner. My colleagues' suggestions have given me most of what I have tried in lecture, and I keep learning from how they teach. Alongside that, I want a higher-resolution picture of how I teach best, so after each class I note how the things I tried went, and I use those notes to decide what to keep and how to adjust it. This fall the committee and I have talked about fitting these practices to the way I teach.

Every position comes with defined expectations: a job description, and the guidance of colleagues who have been doing this work far longer than I have. Meeting those expectations well was my first priority this year, and I worked hard at it. But I also found work that no one had assigned, work I saw a need for and knew I could do. I took it from an idea to something others now use, and I grew more through that process than through anything else this year. This reflection follows the same four sections as last year's, with both kinds of work in view. Teaching Philosophy Last year I ended this section with a goal: "to find the balance between stability and curiosity—between comfort and challenge." Three years of observation reports gave me specific things to work on, and I prepared this fall's first observed lab around them. The slides said where each value should be recorded, students had a checklist to mark at the bench, and twice during the lab they explained a step to a neighbor. The procedure for that experiment had changed from a volumetric pipet to a graduated cylinder. In earlier terms I announced changes like this aloud, and students missed them. This time I had students open the manual with me, find the step, and write the change in. I also rewrote my teaching philosophy this year. It describes teaching as setting the conditions that make learning more likely across a whole section. The full statement is on the Teaching Philosophy page. Technology Integration Last year I wrote that I planned "to experiment with MyOpenMath, Plickers, and Playlab." I tried all three. I ran the CHEM V120B pre-labs on MyOpenMath for a summer term and did not continue with it afterward. I watched Plickers work well in a colleague's class and have not used it in mine so far. I built a project guide in PlayLab for a CHEM V120B final project, and it remains a prototype. Each is described on the Tools I Tried page. The larger change this year was in how I use AI. Once I moved from asking questions in a chat window to having an agent work inside my own files, I could build things I had only been able to describe before. I learned SQL and retrieval-augmented generation because the work called for them. The database of my teaching materials and the thirty-five interactive simulations for CHEM V101 came out of that work. These are on the AI Integration and CHEM V101 Interactive Simulations pages. Teaching Methodology The work I started on my own reached the classroom in several places. The lab quizzes ask about the work done at the bench. For Experiment 2, students marked a one-page checklist while they worked, and every question on the next week's quiz corresponded to at least one box on it. In lecture, students now explain a step aloud to a partner while working a problem. I planned this for the middle of an explanation, and in practice it has settled at the moment a practice block opens. Other changes came from feedback. After a colleague suggested demonstrations in lecture, I ran one on limiting reactants and then moved that idea into a simulation. Another colleague suggested sharing student work on the document camera. I tried it in lecture. The observer that day recorded the comparison as a strength, and my own experience of it was different. When the solution on the screen is correct, there is little for me to add beyond praise, so the method gives me something to teach only when a student's solution is wrong, and that student then has the error shown to the whole room. I was uneasy about that. It also broke up the way I run lecture. I teach from an iPad, and each time I had to switch to the overhead camera and back and have a student's paper passed up to me across a small classroom. I stopped showing individual students' work. I also noticed that when I zoom into part of a slide, students can lose their place, so I am changing my slides to show the whole page first and zoom afterward. Reflective Analysis When I follow AI, I mostly read developer sources: new features in the frontier models, projects on GitHub and Hugging Face, material written by and for developers and companies. That field moves quickly, and keeping up with it for its own sake could carry me away into the technology. So I keep two rules. What I build should be easy to share, and when I work with colleagues I follow the schedule we all keep. In nearly every project I wrote to my colleagues first, laid out how I planned to proceed, and reported as I went. When I volunteered to reorganize the chemistry department's shared Canvas course, each bulk change was shown as a table before anything moved, nothing was deleted, and a page generated from the change log lets colleagues find where their files went. Reading three years of observation reports side by side, I see that organization and clarity were named as strengths in my first year and have stayed, and that each year's feedback pushed toward a room with more student participation. My first-, third- and fourth-year evaluations have recommended that I move around the room more, and I have thought carefully about how to respond. I teach lecture from an iPad at the front, which I consider one of my strengths, and the room is laid out like a small theater, with little space to walk between rows. I also believe students need time to work through problems on their own, without someone hovering over them. So I treat the two parts of class differently: during lecture I stay at the front, where the iPad lets me teach most effectively, and during practice time I circulate through the room to check in with students and answer questions. This year I learned the tools and began applying them to my teaching. From here I want to keep bringing ideas of my own and building them, in ways that help my students and my colleagues.
